definition: Heinous means shockingly wicked — describing an act or crime so evil that it provokes outrage.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word heinous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know heinous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Even veteran detectives were shaken by so heinous a crime.
Calling an act wrong notes a moral failure, but calling it heinous means it is so evil that it shocks people.
Unspeakable is even stronger than heinous — the act is so horrifying that people can barely bring themselves to discuss it.

Atrocious marks acts and conditions as shockingly cruel or dreadfully bad — atrocious crimes, atrocious cruelty. Like heinous it attaches to the deed rather than the doer, but it has also gone soft in casual use (atrocious traffic, atrocious spelling); heinous never jokes, and always means real moral horror.

Abominable centers on the disgust a thing provokes — it turns the stomach and invites moral revulsion. Heinous centers on the outrage: an act so shockingly wicked that people cry out against it. An abominable practice repels you; a heinous crime makes people demand justice.

Monstrous means outrageously evil or cruel, and it is the word that stretches to cover the doer as well as the deed — English speaks easily of a monstrous tyrant. Heinous stays pinned to the act itself: a monstrous man commits heinous crimes, not the other way round.

Heinous reached English through Old French haine, 'hatred' — a word the French themselves had borrowed from the same ancient Germanic root that gives us hate. So a heinous act is, quite literally, a hate-filled one.
Heinous means shockingly wicked — describing an act or crime so evil that it provokes outrage.
The jury agreed that locking the workers inside the burning factory was a heinous act, far beyond ordinary negligence.
Heinous marks the specific act itself as so evil it shocks — the sentence contrasts it with mere negligence to show the moral outrage the word carries.
Heinous describes a specific act or crime so evil it provokes shock — 'a heinous crime' is the classic collocation.
It describes the act itself, not a person's ongoing character (for a person, a word like monstrous fits better).
A related but distinct word in this unit, depravity, is a noun naming someone's underlying corrupt moral nature rather than any one shocking act.
